title: Service-repository pattern

overview.why: It makes testing much easier. You can test the Service's rules without needing a real database by giving it a fake Repository.

why_learning_this: It is the industry standard for writing maintainable backend code.
It allows you to switch databases easily in the future without changing business logic.

common_mistakes.title: Putting logic in the Repository
common_mistakes.explanation: Checking if a user's name is long enough inside the repository. The repository should be dumb; it just saves data.

common_mistakes.title: Writing SQL in the Service
common_mistakes.explanation: Writing database queries directly in the service class. The service should call `repo.get_user()` instead.

recall_questions.q: Explain the Service-Repository pattern in your own words, as if to a classmate.
recall_questions.answer: It is a way to split jobs: the Service makes business decisions, and the Repository only handles saving and finding data in the database.

recall_questions.q: Why is it bad to put business logic inside the Repository?
recall_questions.answer: Because the repository's only job is to interact with the database, like a filing clerk. The service should make the decisions.

recall_questions.q: How does this pattern help with testing?
recall_questions.answer: You can test the Service's business rules by using a fake repository, so you don't need a real database running.

understanding_checks.question: What does this print?
understanding_checks.why: The Service calls the `save` method on the Repository object it was given, which returns the string.

understanding_checks.question: If we want to change our app from a SQL database to a MongoDB database, which class do we rewrite?
understanding_checks.why: Because the Repository handles all data storage. The Service does not know or care what type of database is used.
